# User Guide

Purpose: explain every screen of Longstead, what each number means, which assumptions the app makes, and what it does not model.

Longstead does its calculations on your iPhone or Mac, and by default its AI advisors run there too. The tax, required-minimum-distribution (RMD), Social Security, withdrawal and simulation figures come from the app's own fixed code and bundled tax tables. The AI advisors explain and discuss those figures; they are not the calculator. See [AI_AND_MODELS.md](AI_AND_MODELS.md).

## How the app is laid out

On **iPhone** a tab bar at the bottom has five tabs: **Plan**, **Accounts**, **Simulate**, **Withdraw**, and **Council**. The gear icon at the top right of **Plan** opens **Settings**. **Profile** is reached from the **Plan** screen's **Quick Links**, and from Settings under **Edit profile**.

On **Mac** (and iPad) the same screens are reached from a sidebar. From top to bottom:

- **Your account.** The app opens here at launch and after every unlock.
- **Your picture.** Collapsed by default, with an "N more" chip. Click the chip or the arrow to expand it. Inside: Plan, Debts, Income, Other assets, Goals, Dependents, Assumptions, Reports, Stress test and Scenarios.
- **Simulate**, **Withdraw** and **Council**.
- Below a divider: **Profiles** and **Settings**.
- **Guided setup**, always at the bottom.

There are no separate **Accounts** or **Profile** entries in the sidebar any more: **Your account** covers both. The setup flow appears the first time you open the app.

#### Your account

**Your account** shows a summary of your profile, including **Spending per year**, with an **Update profile** button. Below it are your accounts with an **Add account** button, which is shown even when you have none yet.

#### Your picture

**Your picture** is the rest of your financial picture. Its screen has a **What you spend** row (Spending per year, with **Add** or **Change**). The other items listed above open from the same group.

The app always uses a dark appearance.

The current plan is the **active** plan. Everything on screen (accounts, simulation, withdrawals, Council context) uses the active plan. See [Plans](#plans-projects).

## Plan (home)

Title: **Retirement**. From top to bottom:

- **Today.** The total of all your account balances in the active plan, or a dash if you have no accounts. A **Run simulation** link opens **Simulate**. The "YoY" tag is a placeholder; no growth figure is shown here.
- **Allocation.** A donut chart and percentages of your balance by tax treatment (Tax-Deferred, Tax-Free, Taxable, Tax-Exempt). It appears once you have accounts.
- **Plans.** Your plans. Tap the circle to make a plan active. Tap the chevron to open the plan's detail screen (rename, archive, delete, view analyses).
- **Quick Links.** **Profile** and **Accounts**.

## Accounts

Lists every account in the active plan.

- **Total balance** and **Annual flow in** (contributions plus employer match across all accounts).
- A bar showing the share of your balance that is "tax-advantaged" (everything except Taxable).
- A grouping control: **By tax**, **By type** (account type) and **By bank** (institution; accounts without one go under "No institution").
- Tap an account to edit it. Swipe an account to delete it.

### Adding or editing an account

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Name | Required. For example "Vanguard 401(k)". |
| Type | 401(k), Roth 401(k), Traditional IRA, Roth IRA, Rollover IRA, SEP IRA, 403(b), 457(b), Taxable Brokerage, Personal Trading Account, HSA, Savings Account, Certificate of Deposit, Pension, Annuity, Employee Stock Purchase Plan, Restricted Stock Units, Other. Homes and other property go under Other assets, pensions and annuities under Income. |
| Tax treatment | Tax-Deferred (taxed on withdrawal), Tax-Free (Roth), Taxable, Tax-Exempt (HSA). It pre-fills from the account type (401(k), 403(b), 457(b), IRAs, pension, annuity: Tax-Deferred; Roth: Tax-Free; HSA: Tax-Exempt; everything else: Taxable) until you choose one yourself; editing an existing account never overwrites your choice. |
| Institution | Optional label. |
| Balance | Required, zero or more. |
| Annual contribution, Employer match | Added to the portfolio each year until your retirement age. |
| Expected return | Stored with the account. The Simulate screen does not use it; it applies one return assumption to the whole portfolio. |
| Notes | Free text. |

Accounts are the investable savings the plan can spend. Homes, rentals and other property (Other assets) count toward net worth only. Pensions and annuities are entered as Income. Debts are entered under Debts; their monthly payments are added to your spending in the plan. The Home screen shows a net worth card and a "Finish your plan" checklist ("Your picture" in the sidebar) where you add each item or tap **I have none**. The small **i** buttons explain each section.

### Your plan name, the profile menu and the profile check

- **Your plan: <name>.** The top of Home shows the active plan's name with a pencil. Tap it to **rename** the plan (the name is trimmed, cannot be empty, and is limited to 60 characters). A new plan is called "My Plan"; the first time you type your own name in Profile, the plan takes that name, unless you already renamed it yourself.
- **Profile menu.** Next to it (and at the top of the Mac sidebar) a menu with your name and a chevron is always visible, even with one profile. It lists every profile with a checkmark on the active one, then **Rename...**, **Add someone...** and **Switch user...**. A password-protected profile still asks for its password. You can also rename from the **Profiles** list (touch and hold, or right-click) and from the "Who's using" screen.
- **Set up your profile first.** Until your profile has a name, your current age and your retirement age (nothing is assumed), every Add button, **Import statement**, **I have none** and the Home links to Accounts, Debts, Income, Other assets, Goals and Dependents are turned off, and each screen says **Set up your profile first** with a button to the Profile form. Guided setup starts by asking for these basics.
- **Guided setup is always there.** Home shows a **Start guided setup** (or **Continue**) card until you finish, answer every question, or tap the x to hide it. It is also in Settings, in Home's Quick Links, in **Your picture**, and as **Guided setup** at the bottom of the Mac sidebar.

### Guided setup ("Walk me through it")

When you first set up, choose **Walk me through it** or **I know what to add** (Quick entry). The guided setup asks one plain question at a time: workplace retirement plans, IRAs, brokerage, cash, HSA, company stock, pension, annuity, Social Security (and your spouse's if you file jointly), your home and mortgage, other property and income, each kind of debt, people you support, goals and health coverage. Each question says why it is asked and where to find the number. Answer **Yes** to open the normal entry form (then **Add another** or **Done with this**), **No** if you have none, or **Not sure** to leave it empty; Not sure items stay on your missing list and the planner assumes nothing for them. Back and Skip never save anything. **Save and exit** keeps your place; Home shows **Continue guided setup** until you finish. The **Added so far** panel (a chip on iPhone) shows total assets, debts and net worth as you go. The last step lists everything you entered, where each row can be edited or deleted, with your completeness score. You can offer a statement import on account and debt questions; it still shows what it read for you to check before saving. Guided and Quick entry fill in the same lists, so you can switch at any time, from the menu in the guided setup or from the checklist.

### Goals, dependents and assumptions

- **Goals** (sidebar, or Quick Links on Home): college, a home purchase, a trip, family help, long-term care. Enter the cost per year in today's dollars, your age when it starts and how many years it lasts. Goals that fall in your retired years are added to spending in Simulate, Withdraw and the advisors. Goals before your retirement age are saved and shown to the advisors but not yet modeled.
- **Dependents**: people you support (children, grandchildren, parents). Enter the yearly cost and the age you stop. Same retired-years rule as goals. Do not also count these costs in Annual spending.
- **Assumptions**: your own inflation rate, return after inflation, volatility, and the yearly change in real spending after retirement (for example -1% if you expect to spend less as you age). Empty boxes use the app's defaults; Reset to defaults clears them.

### Health care and your spouse

- **Health care** (Profile, Health care and household): choose how you will be insured before 65 (ACA marketplace, COBRA, retiree or employer plan, no insurance, or "already included in my spending") and your Medicare setup from 65 (Original Medicare with Medigap and Part D, or Medicare Advantage). The planner adds estimated premiums and out-of-pocket costs on top of your spending, growing with health care inflation (general inflation plus 1.5 points unless you set a rate on the Assumptions screen). Enter your own premium or out-of-pocket amounts to replace the estimates. Keep health costs out of Annual spending, or choose "already included". Your HSA pays medical costs first, tax-free, and is otherwise drawn last.
- **Spouse and joint planning** (married filing jointly): spouse age, retirement age, life expectancy, the age your spouse claims Social Security, and optionally exact birth years. The plan runs to the age the last of you is expected to live. A lower-earning spouse can receive up to half of the other's full benefit; after the first death the survivor keeps the larger Social Security benefit, and spending drops to the percentage you set. Required withdrawals start at 73 (born 1951 to 1959) or 75 (born 1960 or later) from your birth year, with a longer joint-life divisor when your spouse is more than 10 years younger.

## Simulate

A Monte Carlo simulation: the app runs thousands of random "what if markets behave differently" futures and counts how many keep your money from running out.

What you see:

1. **Plan health.** The percentage of simulated paths that stay funded through your horizon age, with the number of paths and the age. Colour: green at 80% or more, amber at 60% to under 80%, red below 60%. Before a result exists it shows a dash.
2. **Monte Carlo portfolio range.** A fan chart of portfolio value by calendar year in today's dollars. The dark line is the median. The inner band is the 25th to 75th percentile, and the outer band is the 10th to 90th percentile. Drag across the chart to read a year. A marker shows your retirement year.
3. **Simulation assessment.** A fixed, rule-based summary (it is not AI generated): a headline ("Plan holds up in most simulated paths", "Plan has a meaningful depletion risk", or "Plan depletes in many simulated paths"), the median ending balance, and the 10th to 90th percentile range at your horizon age.
4. **Assumptions.** Sliders for real return (0% to 10%), volatility (5% to 25%), retirement age (50 to 75) and horizon (80 to 105). The starting values come from your profile and accounts; return and volatility start from your risk tolerance (Conservative 3% and 8%, Moderate 5% and 12%, Aggressive 7% and 16%) and are left to your sliders until you change the risk tolerance again. The sliders do not change your saved profile.
5. **Run again.** Runs the simulation again. It uses a fixed random seed, so the same inputs give the same result every time; the number only changes when you change an input. The app also re-runs it automatically, with the same 10,000 paths, a moment after you move a slider.

Where the inputs come from:

- Starting balance: the sum of all account balances.
- Contribution: the sum of annual contributions and employer matches, until retirement.
- Spending: your profile's annual spending (required: the plan shows no success estimate until it is entered), plus the monthly payments of any debts you entered.
- Social Security: your expected monthly amount plus your spouse's, times 12, starting at your claim age.
- Ages: from your profile. If your profile has a retirement age below 50 or above 75, or a life expectancy below 80 or above 105, the slider uses the nearest allowed value.

The paths are random draws, but the app uses a fixed seed, so the same inputs always give the same result. Results change only when you change an input (for example a slider or your profile). The full run takes a few seconds on a recent device.

## Withdraw

Needs a profile and at least one account; otherwise the screen offers **Edit profile** and **Add accounts**.

The Withdraw screen is a planning view, not a year-by-year tax projection. It splits retirement into four phases and shows which kinds of account the money would come from.

- **Lifetime path.** A timeline from your current age to your horizon with the four phases marked.
- **Phase picker.** **Bridge**, **Pre-RMD**, **RMD**, **Late**. See [phases](#bridge-pre-rmd-rmd-and-late-phases).
- **Phase detail.** The ages in the phase, the yearly amount to draw, and a **Source mix** bar split by Tax-Deferred, Taxable, Tax-Free and Tax-Exempt.
- **Recommended order.** A general checklist: required minimum distributions, tax-deferred accounts, Roth conversions in low-bracket years, taxable accounts, Roth, then HSA. The first row is greyed out in phases before RMDs begin. This list is general guidance and is not re-ordered for your numbers. The Source mix bar follows its own order: in the Bridge phase it draws from Taxable, then Tax-Deferred, then Tax-Free, then Tax-Exempt (HSA); in later phases it draws Tax-Deferred first, then Taxable, Tax-Free, Tax-Exempt.

The comparison card below the checklist projects all three withdrawal orders year by year and shows lifetime tax and the balance left at the end for each; the one you pick is saved with your plan and used by the advisors. The Source mix does not grow balances, apply taxes or adjust for inflation. It shows only how today's balances would cover the spending need, phase by phase. The year-by-year projection with tax is the comparison card; advisors using a downloaded (MLX) model can run the same projection from your profile. The Apple on-device path does not have that calculator.

### Medicare and ACA income limits, long-term care, and retirement taxes

- **Income limits card (Withdraw).** For each retired year it shows the Medicare premium surcharge (IRMAA) your income would trigger two years later, how much room is left under the next tier, and, before 65 on marketplace coverage, how close you are to the 400% poverty-level subsidy cliff and how much credit you would lose by going over. You can type "add income of $X in the year I am N" to see the effect of a Roth conversion or a big withdrawal; it changes that one year only. Choosing **Bracket fill** adds a switch to keep income under the ACA cliff.
- **IRMAA.** Part B plus Part D surcharges per person on Medicare, set by income from two years earlier. The first retired years have no earlier modeled year, so the first projected income stands in. Thresholds grow with inflation. After a spouse dies, the survivor uses the single table from the next year.
- **ACA credit.** Before 65 on marketplace coverage the credit is your plan premium less a share of income that rises with income. Under current law (2026 data) the credit ends the moment income is over 400% of the poverty level; the temporary 2021-2025 rules had no cliff. Income for this test includes the untaxed part of Social Security and realized gains. If Congress changes the law this will be out of date.
- **Long-term care (Assumptions, Simulate).** Enter a start age, number of years, yearly cost in today's dollars, cost inflation and any insurance benefit, then switch it on. Simulate shows the chance of success with and without the care. If you also enter a Long-term care goal under Goals, both are counted: use one or the other.
- **Taxes in the projection.** The 3.8% net investment income tax on gains and rental income above $200,000 ($250,000 joint, not inflation indexed), a 10% penalty on tax-deferred withdrawals before 59 and a half (exceptions such as Rule of 55 and 72(t) are not modeled), and the 2025-2028 senior deduction of $6,000 per person 65 or older (reduced by 6% of income over $75,000, $150,000 joint; none from 2029). A survivor files as single from the year after a death.

### Stress test, guardrail spending, scenarios and Roth conversions

- **Stress test (Home, sidebar).** Replays your plan against every real starting year since 1928 (US stocks, 10-year Treasury bonds and cash in your own mix, from the NYU Stern / Damodaran tables, adjusted for inflation) and against retiring into 2000, 2008 or 1966. It shows the share of start years that lasted and the worst one. The first simulated year gets the first historical year, so the sequences start today, not at retirement; the three named sequences start in your first retired year. History is not a forecast. Taxes, health costs and income match Simulate.
- **Guardrail spending (Simulate, Stress test).** A simplified Guyton-Klinger rule: spending is cut 10% when your withdrawal rate climbs more than 20% above where it started, raised 10% when it falls more than 20% below, and the inflation raise is skipped after a losing year. Cuts stop in the last 15 years. It usually improves the chance of lasting but spending varies; the median and the unlucky 1-in-10 spending are shown.
- **Scenarios.** Name a what-if (retire at 67, spend less, claim later, another withdrawal order, different returns, guardrails) that only changes what you fill in. Compare the saved plan plus up to two scenarios side by side. Scenarios never change your saved plan, are saved with the profile and travel in its export file.
- **Roth conversion plan (Withdraw).** For each year before required withdrawals start, it fills the bracket you choose using your real income (pensions, taxable Social Security, other income, required withdrawals), and stops short of a Medicare surcharge tier or the ACA subsidy cliff when stepping across costs too much. Each row shows the tax cost, what limited it, the years to break even, and the age the converted money is free of the 5-year rule. Taxes are assumed paid from money outside the IRA, and the later years are not re-run with the conversions.

### States, future tax years, tax law and statement import

- **All 50 states and DC.** The Tax brackets screen lists every state with its type, data year (2025), confidence and a one-line rule for Social Security, retirement income and capital gains. Low-confidence states carry a tag and a warning; please check them against your state's tax department.
- **Future years.** Brackets, standard deductions and exemptions after the data year are raised each year by your inflation assumption (the plan's Taxes line says so). Statutory amounts that are not indexed (the Social Security taxation thresholds, the 3.8% investment tax thresholds, the senior deduction, which ends after 2028) are left alone.
- **Federal tax law (Plan assumptions).** Default is current law. "Sunset" is only a what-if that assumes the pre-2018 federal rates and deductions return from 2026; its numbers are an estimate, not law, and results say so.
- **Import statement (Accounts and Debts).** Choose a PDF or photo of a brokerage, bank, retirement or loan statement. It is read on your device only (no network, no AI model); you see what was found with the statement line it came from, can edit any field, and nothing is saved until you tap Add. Fields that cannot be read stay empty. Check each value: scanned text can be misread.

## Reports

Open **Reports** from the sidebar (Mac, iPad) or from Quick Links on **Plan** (iPhone). It shows the active profile only, in three tabs:

- **Balance sheet:** what you own (accounts by tax type, then other assets), what you owe, and net worth. Net worth is the same number as on the Plan screen. A mortgage linked to a home also shows the home's equity once; the loan is not subtracted twice.
- **Cash flow:** year by year from today to your planning age, in future dollars, using the withdrawal strategy saved on the Withdraw screen. Each year shows income, withdrawals by account type, spending (living, debt payments, health care, goals), tax, growth and the ending balance. A red row means that year's spending was not fully funded; the balance stops at zero and the CSV has a Shortfall column. Before retirement only saving and growth are shown. The profile has one spending number, so spending is not split into essential and discretionary.
- **Summary:** the chance your savings last (the same 10,000-path run as Simulate), first shortfall age, tax over retirement, ending balance, cash on hand and the assumptions used. If something needed is missing the tab says what to add instead of showing numbers.

**Export** (top right): balance sheet CSV, cash flow CSV, full report as PDF or HTML, or share a text summary. CSV files hold plain numbers (no $ signs or thousands separators), so a spreadsheet can add them up. Every file carries the profile name, the date and a disclaimer. The PDF is Letter size, black on white, for printing. On Mac a Save dialog asks where to put the file. The **Plan health** row on Plan shows the chance it lasts, plan completeness and cash on hand; tap it to open Reports. In **Council** you can ask the planner advisor to summarize your plan and it will quote the same figures.

## Council (AI advisors)

The **Council** tab lists your advisors. A status card at the top says where the AI runs (on this device by default; on your own server if you connect one). Each advisor card shows which model will answer: "Apple built-in AI model (default)", "MLX" followed by the model name, or "Your server" followed by the model name.

| Advisor | What it is for |
| --- | --- |
| **Retirement Planner** | Long-term plan and scenarios: withdrawal order, Roth conversion planning, Social Security timing, RMD planning, sequence-of-returns risk. |
| **Tax Consultant** | Federal and state tax, brackets, standard deduction, capital gains, Social Security taxation, RMDs, Roth conversion room. The advisor to use for any tax figure. |
| **Investment Advisor** | Asset allocation, rebalancing, bond laddering and glide paths. |
| **Devil's Advocate** | Challenges your plan: weak assumptions, bad-market scenarios, overlooked risks. Also has the tax calculators. |
| **Code Generator** | Writes Python code for simulations and calculations. Its output is not connected to the app and is not number-checked. |
| **OCR** | Listed as "Read documents". In this version there is no way to attach an image or file to a chat, so use it as a text-only chat. |

The Retirement Planner is sent only a pass/fail check of the required inputs plus your question, not your profile text, so it does not recite your profile. Its plan figures come from the planning engine. The other advisors see your active profile and account list as context (name, ages, filing status, state, spending, Social Security, and each account's name, type, balance and contribution), together with the engine's computed facts. By default that information stays on your device; if an advisor is set to your own model server, it is sent to that server. The context also includes your debts, income sources, other assets and a "Plan completeness" percentage.

**Missing items open the exact field.** Tapping a missing item (Home list, the Set up profile button, the Fix this link under an advisor's accuracy note, Your picture) opens the screen and takes you to the exact field: the Profile form scrolls to it, highlights it and puts the cursor in it, and a list screen opens its add form. Until your name, current age and retirement age are set, every item takes you to those first. In Profile, each required field that is still empty shows a Needed note, and the top row says how many details are still needed and jumps to the next one. A stepper reads Not set until you change it.

**Plan completeness.** The Home screen has a Plan completeness card with a percentage and up to six missing items; tap a row to open the screen where you add it. The score is calculated by the app (never by the AI): core plan details (ages, spending, accounts with a balance, filing status, state) are 50 points, Debts 15, Income 15, Social Security and health plan 10, home 5, other assets 3 and goals 2. For Debts, Income, Social Security, home, Other assets and Goals, tapping **I have none** counts as complete. New profiles start with filing status, state and health plan already filled with defaults, so they begin around 21%; when filing jointly, spouse age is also asked for.

**Required and optional details.** Five things block a plan figure: current age, retirement age, yearly spending, filing status, and savings in at least one account. Everything else (Social Security, debts, income, other assets, home, goals, health costs) is optional: it improves accuracy and is listed in the accuracy note, but it never blocks an answer. A value you state in your question is not treated as missing.

**Accuracy note.** Whenever the plan is below 100%, each advisor reply starts with a small note written by the app, not by the AI: "this answer uses N% of the details a full plan needs. Not yet entered: ...". If the advisor needs something you have not entered to give a number about your own plan (for example accounts for the Retirement Planner, or income for the tax advisors), the note adds "I can't give a reliable figure for your plan yet because ... is missing. Please add it in ..., then ask again." The note is not saved with the conversation, so replies you reopen later do not show it. The advisors also state the assumption they used for each missing detail, and they will not call a plan complete.

**Questions about your own totals.** Advisors running on a downloaded (MLX) model can look up your net worth, monthly debt payments, total income and plan completeness directly from your entered data. If a section is empty and you have not tapped I have none, they ask you to add it instead of guessing.

### Chatting

- Tap an advisor to open a chat. Before your first message, tappable example questions appear.
- Type your question and send it. Use the stop button to cancel an answer in progress.
- Tap **Listen** under a finished answer to hear it read aloud with your device's built-in voice.
- The sparkles button explains the Listen feature and how to ask iOS to summarize the screen.
- The menu at the top right has **Clear thread** (deletes that advisor's messages for the active plan), **Export conversation...** (copy as Markdown, share as text, or save as PDF) and **Settings**.
- **Short memory.** The advisor remembers your last two exchanges in the chat (each shortened), so a brief follow-up works. It does not remember anything older, and a cleared thread is forgotten. For anything important, restate the year, filing status, state and amounts.
- Answers on the Apple path are limited in length (about 500 tokens), so they are short by design.
- **Chat header.** It reads "Apple built-in AI model (default)", "MLX - <model>" or "Your server - <model>". While Apple's model is in use and nothing else is set up, a banner explains the options; you can dismiss it and the app remembers.
- **My plan numbers (no AI).** In the Retirement Planner chat this button posts the planning engine's figures instantly with no model involved, labelled "Planning engine (no AI)". It is exact and repeatable. If a required input is missing it names it instead.
- **Your own model server.** If Ollama is running, the app finds it, connects, and sets each advisor's default model; the header shows a notice with **Change models** and **Use Apple's built-in model instead**. You can also connect Ollama, LM Studio or another server yourself in **Settings > Your own model server**. See [AI_AND_MODELS.md](AI_AND_MODELS.md).

How the numbers are checked is explained in [AI_AND_MODELS.md](AI_AND_MODELS.md).


## Profile

Open **Profile** from the Plan tab's Quick Links, from Settings under **Edit profile**, or, on Mac and iPad, from **Update profile** under **Your account**. Changes are held until you tap **Save**; **Revert** discards them.

| Section | Fields |
| --- | --- |
| Project | The name of the active plan (read-only here). |
| Identity | Name; current age (18 to 100); retirement age (40 to 90); life expectancy (50 to 120). The ages adjust each other so that current age < retirement age < life expectancy. |
| Tax | Filing status; State (all 50 states and DC, stored as a two-letter code). |
| Spending per year | Yearly spending (monthly spending x 12), after tax, in today's dollars. Do not include payments you enter under Debts or health insurance and medical costs; the plan adds those. |
| Social Security | Claim age (62 to 70); expected monthly benefit; spouse's monthly benefit. |
| Other | Risk tolerance (Conservative, Moderate, Aggressive). Advisors can see it, and it sets the starting return and volatility on Simulate (see below). |
| Plan management | **Export plan...**, **Import plan...**, **Duplicate plan**, **Reset plan**. |

### Plan management

- **Export plan...** saves the active plan (profile and accounts) as a `.retplan` file that you can keep in Files, AirDrop to another device, or email to yourself. The file is plain, unencrypted text: it contains your name, ages and balances, so store it as carefully as a financial statement.
- **Import plan...** reads a `.retplan` file and adds it as a **new** plan, which becomes the active plan. A file from a newer version of the app, or with unrecognized values, is rejected with a message and nothing is imported.
- **Duplicate plan** makes a copy named "<name> copy" and makes it active. Use it for what-if versions.
- **Reset plan** deletes the active plan, its profile, accounts, chat history and saved analyses, after a confirmation. This cannot be undone. Export first if you want a copy.

Exports do not include chat history, saved analyses, settings, or downloaded AI models.

## Plans (projects)

You can keep several plans, for example "Base case" and "Retire at 62". Exactly one is active.

- **iPhone:** switch plans from **Plan** (tap the circle next to a plan). New plans come from **Duplicate plan** or **Import plan...** in Profile. Tapping a plan's chevron opens its detail: rename, **Make active**, **Archive**, **Delete project**, and **View analyses**.
- **Mac / iPad:** the **Projects** screen has a **+** button for **New Project**, swipe actions (Activate, Archive, Delete), and an Archived section. On Mac, **File > New Project...** (Command-N) creates a plan named "New plan" followed by today's date and makes it active, and the same menu lists your plans so you can switch.

**View analyses** lists the questions and answers saved from your Council chats for that plan, with the advisor and model that produced each one.

## Numbers explained

### Plan health, success rate and trials

The simulation draws a random yearly return for every year of your plan, thousands of times. A path "succeeds" if the balance never drops below zero before your horizon age. **Success rate** and **plan health** are the same number: successful paths divided by total paths. 82% does not mean "82% sure"; it means that, under the assumptions on screen, 82 of every 100 simulated futures stayed funded. It is a scenario estimate, not a forecast or guarantee.

### Percentile bands

For each year, the app sorts all simulated balances from lowest to highest. The **median (50th percentile)** is the middle one. The **25th to 75th** band holds the middle half of outcomes. The **10th to 90th** band holds the middle 80%. A path at the 10th percentile did worse than 90% of the others. Values are in today's dollars.

### Bridge, Pre-RMD, RMD and Late phases

The Withdraw screen computes four phases from your profile:

- **Bridge:** from your retirement age until your Social Security claim age (if you claim at or before retirement, this phase is empty). Spending is covered entirely from savings.
- **Pre-RMD:** from the end of Bridge until required minimum distributions begin. Social Security is subtracted from the spending need.
- **RMD:** from the RMD start age until age 80 (or the RMD start age if it is later than 80).
- **Late:** from the end of the RMD phase to your horizon age.

### RMD age 73 versus 75

Under the SECURE 2.0 Act, required minimum distributions from tax-deferred accounts start at age **73** for people born before 1960, and at age **75** for people born in 1960 or later. The app uses the birth year in your Profile; if it is blank it estimates it as this year minus your current age. The amount for a year is the account balance divided by the IRS Uniform Lifetime Table divisor for your age (for example, 26.5 at age 73 and 24.6 at age 75). If your spouse is the sole beneficiary of the account and is more than 10 years younger than you, the IRS Joint Life table gives a larger divisor and a smaller required amount; the app applies it while your spouse is alive (exact for owners 73-80 with spouses 55-64, a close estimate elsewhere).

### Social Security claiming

You choose a claim age from 62 to 70 and enter your expected monthly benefit. The Simulate and Withdraw screens use your entered amount from the claim age onward, unchanged, in today's dollars. They do not reduce it for claiming early or increase it for claiming late, so enter the amount for the age you actually intend to claim.

When you ask the Retirement Planner or Tax Consultant to compare claiming ages, the app's calculator treats your entered benefit as the amount at **full retirement age (FRA)** and compares claiming at 62, FRA and 70:

- FRA is 66 for birth years up to 1954, rises by 2 months per birth year through 1959, and is 67 for 1960 and later.
- Claiming early reduces the benefit by 5/9 of 1% per month for the first 36 months before FRA and 5/12 of 1% per month beyond that.
- Waiting past FRA adds 8% per year up to age 70.
- It reports monthly and annual benefits, lifetime totals to your life expectancy, and the "breakeven" ages where waiting overtakes claiming earlier.

Up to 85% of Social Security can be taxable. The app uses the IRS "provisional income" method: other income plus half your benefits, with thresholds of $25,000 / $34,000 (single, head of household, qualifying widow(er)) or $32,000 / $44,000 (married filing jointly). These thresholds are fixed by law and are not adjusted for inflation.

### Roth conversion room

"Room" is how much you could convert from a traditional account to a Roth account this year before your taxable income passes the top of a federal bracket you choose (for example, the 24% bracket), together with the federal tax that conversion would cost. Ask the Tax Consultant: "How much can I convert to Roth and stay in the 24% bracket? My income is $X, single, 2026." It uses the standard deduction and the federal bracket table; it does not include state tax, Medicare premium surcharges, or the effect on Social Security taxation.

### Tax figures

- **Federal tax** uses the bracket tables and standard deduction for the year, filing status and age. The extra deduction for age 65 and older is added only when the age is 65 or more.
- **State tax** uses the bundled state tables (see below), after the state's standard deduction and personal exemption where the data has them.
- **Capital gains** use the 0%, 15% and 20% federal brackets, stacked on top of your other income.
- **Effective rate** is total tax divided by income. **Marginal rate** is the rate on your next dollar.

## Assumptions

| Item | What the app assumes |
| --- | --- |
| Dollars | Simulate works in **real (inflation-adjusted) dollars**. Spending and Social Security stay constant in today's dollars; returns are real returns. |
| Overrides | The **Assumptions** screen can replace the inflation, return and volatility below, and set a yearly change in real spending after retirement. Anything you leave empty uses the default. |
| Return | Starts from your risk tolerance: **3% / 8%** (Conservative), **5% / 12%** (Moderate) or **7% / 16%** (Aggressive) real return and yearly volatility (standard deviation). With no profile, 5% and 15%. Drawn from a normal distribution each year. Adjustable 0% to 10% and 5% to 25%. Accounts with a **Stock share** (Advanced) get their own return and volatility: stocks, bonds and cash defaults are 6.5% / 17%, 2% / 6% and 0.5% real, shown and editable on the Assumptions screen; savings accounts and CDs count as cash. The plan blends them by balance. A plan-wide return you enter replaces the blend. |
| Inflation | 2.5% unless you set your own on the Assumptions screen. Simulate works in real dollars, so inflation only matters for things quoted as fixed dollar amounts (debt payments) and for the Withdraw projection. |
| Timing | Contributions are added every year through your retirement age. Spending starts the year after. Social Security starts at the claim age, even if you are still working. |
| Withdraw screen | No growth, no inflation, no tax. A planning split only. |
| Withdrawal projection (Withdraw screen comparison, Council with downloaded MLX models) | Year by year in future dollars. Balances grow at the plan's inflation plus real return, or each bucket at the blend of its accounts' stock shares. Spending, Social Security and health costs are inflated from today. Order depends on the chosen strategy: **Standard** (taxable, tax-deferred, Roth, HSA last), **Bracket fill** (tax-deferred up to a bracket you pick, then taxable, Roth, HSA) or **Roth last** (taxable, HSA, tax-deferred, Roth). The HSA pays medical costs first, tax-free. Selling a taxable account returns your cost basis untaxed and taxes only the gain at 0, 15 or 20% on top of that year's income; if you did not enter a cost basis, half the balance is assumed to be gain (savings accounts and CDs are never assumed to have a gain). Bracket fill counts the taxable part of Social Security toward the bracket, so total income stays at the top of the bracket you picked. The 3.8% net investment income tax, the 10% early-withdrawal penalty before 59 and a half and the 2025-2028 senior deduction are included. RMDs come first. Tax tables stay at current-year levels and are not inflated. |
| Council simulation (downloaded MLX models only) | The advisors' success-probability tool uses the same plan inputs as the Simulate screen (10,000 paths, fixed seed), so its result is repeatable and matches Simulate. It refuses to answer when your ages, spending or accounts are missing. |
| Tax tables | Federal brackets, standard deductions and capital-gains brackets are bundled for **2024, 2025 and 2026**. State income tax data is bundled for **all 50 states and DC (tax year 2025)**, with each state's own treatment of Social Security, pension and IRA income and capital gains. Every state shows a data year and a confidence level (high, medium or low) on the Tax brackets screen; most states are medium or low because the tables were entered from knowledge, not checked line by line against state publications, so verify yours. Years after the data year use the 2025 tables raised by your inflation assumption. Local taxes (city, county) are not included. |
| Tax updates | The app uses its built-in tables and makes no tax-data requests, unless you enter your own feed address in Settings. See [SETTINGS_GUIDE.md](SETTINGS_GUIDE.md). |
| RMD table | IRS Uniform Lifetime Table, ages 73 to 120. |

You can browse the bundled tables in **Settings > Tax data > View brackets**.

## What the app does not model

Verified against the code. Treat results as estimates and talk to a professional for decisions.

- **Interest and dividends in the Net Investment Income Tax.** The 3.8% tax is applied to realized gains and rental/royalty income only; returns are total return, so interest and dividends are not separated.
- **IRMAA, ACA subsidies and long-term care** are modeled in simplified form (see Withdraw). Not modeled: Medicaid and state subsidies, IRMAA appeals, hardship rules, and the yearly re-indexing of the ACA contribution table. The Monte Carlo on Simulate uses a simpler tax estimate that leaves out the NIIT, the early-withdrawal penalty and the senior deduction.
- **Alternative minimum tax (AMT)**, itemized deductions, tax credits, and above-the-line deductions. Only the standard deduction is used.
- **Payroll taxes** on earnings, and taxes on income you earn while still working.
- **Early-withdrawal penalty exceptions**: Rule of 55, 72(t) payments, disability and others. The 10% penalty is charged on every tax-deferred draw before 59 and a half. The HSA 20% penalty and Roth earnings rules are not modeled.
- **State detail not modeled:** local taxes (Maryland counties, Ohio and Pennsylvania cities, New York City, Indiana counties), state credits (Oregon federal-tax subtraction, California exemption credit), states' extra capital-gains taxes (Washington above $1 million, Maryland over $350,000 of income, Minnesota over $1 million of investment income), and the full pension rules of states marked "Has rules not modeled here" (their tax on pension and IRA income may be overstated). Married filing separately and head of household use the single tables.
- **Bracket indexing** in multi-year withdrawal projections (the bracket tables are not inflated).
- **Health care details**: premiums and out-of-pocket costs are national-average estimates; the ACA credit and IRMAA are approximations (see Withdraw). The joint-life required-withdrawal divisor is an approximation of the IRS table. A survivor files as single from the year after a death in the withdrawal projection.
- **The Expected return box on an account.** It is saved but not used; the Stock share sets an account's return. Also not modeled: inheritances, home sales, goals and dependent costs that fall before your retirement age, and contribution limits. Debts, pensions and annuities are modeled from the Debts and Income screens, but asset growth, planned sale ages, upkeep costs, asset cost basis and survivor percentages are saved without being used in projections yet.
- **Market sequence from history.** Returns are random draws, not replayed from historical data.
- **Guarantees.** A high plan health is not a promise, and a low one is not a verdict.
